newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: African coffee producers aim to cut consumers' stocks.
newsitem.headline: African coffee producers aim to cut consumers' stocks.

text.p: African coffee producers agreed to approach other producers worldwide to propose a scheme for bolstering prices by reducing roaster stocks in consuming countries.

A statement issued after the 36th general assembly of the Inter-African Coffee Organisation (IACO) which ended late Wednesday deplored a current slump in prices, which is squeezing producers' export revenue.
"The assembly decided therefore that it was urgent to give new impetus to the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) and its export programme," it said.
It announced that a ministerial committee composed of Ivory Coast, Uganda and Angola would hold "high level political and diplomatic consultations" with other ACPC members.
Ivorian Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze told Reuters late Wednesday that the aim was to target roasters' stocks.

"We are currently envisaging a new system which will consist quite simply of ensuring that the eight million (60-kg) bags of coffee that they (the roasters) hold, and which is a sort of security stock, should be used more," he said.
Gauze said the talks would begin in Latin America with nations such as world number one Brazil, Costa Rica and Colombia.
Gauze opened the meeting on Monday with a call for an emergency ACPC meeting to discuss tightening the 1996/97 ACPC export limit programme and agree a response to increased exports by non-members.
The final IACO statement said the ACPC export limit scheme had cut stocks in consumer countries to a 20-year low of 8.5 million bags.

But it added, "The Assembly noted that despite favourable factors and discipline observed by ACPC countries, world prices were at unsatisfactory levels around $1,450 and $2,750 a tonne for robusta and arabica respectively."
It highlighted four major problems -- low demand, increased exports by non-ACPC members, changes in roasters' buying strategy and weakening world prices.
The statement added, however, that the African Coffee Rehabilitation Programme was making steady progress, with both productivity and quality improving.
African coffee production was now projected at 17.2 million (60-kg) bags, it added.
It noted efforts by members to control disease.
Gauze on Monday criticised increased production and exports by non-ACPC members Mexico, Vietnam and Guatemala.
The 14-member ACPC accounts for over 80 percent of world production although a handful of medium-sized producer nations are not members.
World coffee prices, which slumped in the early 1990s, soared after frost in Brazil in 1994 but have since slid again.
The ACPC 1996/97 export programme limits members' green coffee exports to 53.5 million 60-kg bags in the year to June 1997.
Gauze said roasters were now tending to hold lower stocks and buy when they needed to.
